resources.string: Red marrow cutaway
Blood cell production in red marrow
Spongy bone
Bony struts surround the spaces occupied by red marrow.
Hematopoietic compartment
Stem and progenitor cells reside among stromal cells near vascular spaces.
Marrow sinusoid
New blood cells enter the circulation across the sinusoidal lining.
Stem cells occupy supportive marrow niches.
Progenitors commit to distinct blood cell lineages.
Precursors mature and megakaryocytes release platelet fragments.
New blood cells enter the marrow sinusoids.
Thymic lobule cutaway
T-cell development in the thymus
Cortex
A dense outer zone contains developing thymocytes and supporting epithelial cells.
Cortical-medullary junction
Precursors arrive via blood vessels near the junction and migrate into the lobule.
Medulla
In the medulla, additional selection helps establish tolerance to self.
Hassall corpuscle
Concentric epithelial layers are a recognizable feature of the thymic medulla.
Blood-borne precursors enter near the cortical-medullary junction.
In the cortex, selection favors cells able to recognize self-MHC.
In the medulla, many strongly self-reactive cells are removed and some become regulatory T cells.
Mature naive T cells leave to circulate through peripheral lymphoid tissues.
Splenic red and white pulp
Two functions of splenic blood filtration
Splenic hilum
Blood vessels enter and leave at the hilum. This is a blood filter, not a filter of incoming lymph.
White pulp
Lymphoid tissue surrounds a small arterial branch and surveys blood-borne material.
Red pulp
The red pulp contains cords and sinusoids. Macrophages remove many aged or altered red cells.
Arterial blood reaches the splenic hilum.
White pulp samples blood-borne material around arterial branches.
Red pulp screens red blood cells and removes many aged cells.
Venous blood leaves the spleen at the hilum.
Lymph node cross-section
Lymph passage through one node
Afferent vessel
Multiple afferent vessels can deliver lymph through the convex capsule.
Subcapsular sinus
The first space reached by lymph lies just under the capsule.
Medullary sinus
Sinus channels converge through the medulla toward the hilum.
Efferent vessel
Lymph leaves the node at the hilum. The nearby blood vessels are a separate route.
Cortical follicles
Many B cells occupy the follicles; the traveling dot depicts lymph, not a lymphocyte.
Lymph enters from an afferent vessel.
Lymph spreads through the subcapsular sinus.
Sinus channels carry lymph past immune cells toward the medulla.
Lymph leaves through an efferent vessel at the hilum.
Collecting lymphatic vessel and valves
One pumping cycle in a collecting lymphatic
Inlet valve
An upstream valve admits fluid during filling when local pressures favor forward flow.
Contractile segment
Smooth muscle in a collecting vessel helps build pressure between valves.
Outlet valve
The downstream valve can open when segment pressure exceeds outlet pressure.
The segment fills when upstream pressure favors inlet flow.
Wall contraction raises pressure and the inlet valve closes.
The outlet valve opens and fluid moves downstream.
The wall relaxes and the outlet valve limits reverse flow.
Thoracic duct return route
Thoracic duct return to the venous angle
Lower trunk inflow
Abdominal lymphatic trunks converge. A cisterna chyli is one common, variable pattern.
Thoracic ascent
The duct ascends near the vertebral column and typically crosses toward the person\'s left.
Left venous angle
A typical outlet is near the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins.
Lower-body and intestinal drainage gathers into abdominal trunks.
Lymph ascends through the chest in the thoracic duct.
The duct typically turns toward the person\'s left in the upper chest.
Lymph returns to venous blood near the left venous angle.
Palatine tonsil section
Immune sampling at the palatine tonsil
Crypt opening
The example shows a palatine crypt opening to the oropharyngeal surface.
Crypt epithelium
The lining brings surface material near resident immune cells.
Lymphoid follicle
Follicles contain B cells that can respond to local antigen signals.
Material from the mouth contacts the tonsil surface.
Crypts bring samples near the lymphoid tissue.
Local antigen presentation can activate lymphocytes.
Activated B cells can support local antibody responses.
Adenoid at the nasopharyngeal roof
Immune sampling at the adenoid
Nasopharyngeal roof
The pharyngeal tonsil sits along the roof and back wall of the nasopharynx.
Mucosal folds
This surface forms folds. It is distinct from the deep palatine crypt shown in the tonsil plate.
Lymphoid tissue
Immune follicles under the surface sample material carried in nasopharyngeal secretions.
Inhaled material reaches the nasopharyngeal mucosa.
The folded surface brings material near the tissue.
Immune cells sample and present selected antigens.
Local responses can include antibody production.
Ileal Peyer patch example
Sampling over a Peyer patch
Follicle-associated epithelium
Specialized M cells in the dome epithelium can carry luminal material to cells below.
Subepithelial dome
Cells below the epithelium receive and process some of the transported material.
B-cell follicle
The follicle is one example of organized gut-associated lymphoid tissue, not the whole gut immune system.
Material in the ileal lumen contacts the dome epithelium.
M cells transport selected samples across the epithelial layer.
Immune cells in the dome receive and process the samples.
Signals in the lymphoid tissue can support tolerance or a mucosal response.
A selected route or region is highlighted. Playback does not show real timing, quantities, or all possible paths.
Anterior view: the person\'s left is drawn on the right. Duct anatomy varies.
Ideal lymphatic valve
A steady ideal one-way element with fixed open resistance. No leakage, active contractions, compliance, or patient measurements.
Forward flow = max(inlet pressure − outlet pressure, 0) ÷ open resistance.
Inlet minus outlet pressure
